# Performance and properties (house standards, version 4)

<!-- generated by tools/build_data.py from synthesis/; edit the source, not this file -->

Animate only compositor-friendly properties, keep per-frame work out of React state and off the React Native JS thread, pick the cheapest tool and treat dropped frames as a regression.

Rules from non-negotiable sources. **must**: never break it without the person's explicit override. **should**: the default; say so when you depart from it. How to change one: `../standards.md`.

### STD-performance-properties-01: Animate only transform and opacity
**must** · web, css, react, react-native, ios, android. Animate movement, size and visibility with transform and opacity only; never animate width, height, margin, padding, top or left (in React Native, also flex and gap), outside the clip-path, accordion-height and childless-width exceptions in STD-performance-properties-02.
- Values: animate: transform, opacity; never-animate-web: width, height, margin, padding, top, left; never-animate-react-native: width, height, margin, padding, flex, top, left, gap; exception: width on an absolutely positioned element with no children; indicator-sample: translateX and width with withTiming, duration 250, EASE_IN_OUT, measured once with onLayout
- Why: transform and opacity skip layout and paint and run on the GPU, while width, height, margin, padding, top and left trigger all three rendering steps (layout, paint and composite), so the animation stutters. In React Native those properties re-run Yoga on every frame for the node and its siblings.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Animate transform and opacity instead (clip-path for reveals); height only for accordions, width only for an absolutely positioned element with no children.
- Sources: S-L19-013, S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-032, S-L19-033, S-L19-025, S-L19-024, S-L19-031, S-L19-020, S-L19-019, S-L19-016, S-L19-015

### STD-performance-properties-02: Only clip-path, accordion height, childless width
**must** · web, css, react, react-native, ios, android. For movement, size and reveals, the only exceptions to transform and opacity are clip-path and accordion height on the web, and width on an absolutely positioned element with no children (a tab pill, a progress fill).
- Values: fourth-property: clip-path; height-exception: accordions only; width-exception: absolutely positioned element with no children
- Why: clip-path does not affect layout, just like transform, and is hardware-accelerated; accordions have no transform equivalent. An absolutely positioned element with no children is out of flow with no layout dependents, so nothing else re-lays-out, and animating its width keeps the corner radius that scaleX would smear.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-010, S-L19-016, S-L19-015, S-L19-030, S-L19-032

### STD-performance-properties-06: Never use transition: all
**must** · web, css, react. Never write transition: all (or Tailwind's transition-all); name the exact properties that transition.
- Values: instead: transition: transform var(--ds-motion-duration-medium) var(--ds-motion-easing-enter)
- Why: transition: all animates unintended properties off the GPU; the animate skill lists it among the automatic blocks in review-animations.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Name the exact properties and take the timing from the motion tokens, for example transition: transform var(--ds-motion-duration-medium) var(--ds-motion-easing-enter).
- Sources: S-L19-013, S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-027

### STD-performance-properties-09: Motion: animate the full transform string
**must** · web, react. In Motion (Framer Motion), animate the full transform string (animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}) instead of the x, y or scale shorthand props.
- Values: do: animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}; dont: animate={{ x: 100 }}
- Why: The shorthands are not hardware-accelerated: they run on the main thread through requestAnimationFrame and drop frames when the browser is loading, scripting or painting, while the full transform string stays smooth.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Use the full transform string, for example animate={{ transform: "translateX(100px)" }}.
- Sources: S-L19-013, S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033

### STD-performance-properties-10: Keep per-frame values out of React state
**must** · react, web, react-native, ios, android. Write per-frame animation values (drag, scroll or pointer position) to ref.current.style or a Motion motion value on the web, or to a Reanimated shared value in React Native; never set React state per frame.
- Values: web: ref.current.style; motion: motion values (useTransform, useMotionTemplate) passed as inline style; react-native: shared value + useAnimatedStyle
- Why: Setting state every frame re-renders the component every frame, the single biggest cause of jank in React Native apps. Motion values update inline styles without re-rendering, so keep scroll-driven values as motion values end to end: copied into a const they stop receiving updates.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Per-frame value in React state: write it to ref.current.style, a motion value or a shared value.
- Sources: S-L19-013, S-L19-005, S-L19-010, S-L19-016

### STD-performance-properties-11: Set drag transforms on the moving element
**must** · web, css, react. During drags and other per-frame updates, set transform directly on the moving element (element.style.transform = `translateY(${distance}px)`); never drive it through a CSS variable set on a parent or container.
- Values: do: element.style.transform = `translateY(${distance}px)`; dont: element.style.setProperty('--swipe-amount', `${distance}px`); lag-seen-at: ~20 list items; react: ref.current.style
- Why: CSS variables are inheritable, so changing one recalculates styles for every child; the drawer's drag became laggy once it held more than about 20 list items, and setting the transform on the element fixed it.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Drag offset set through a CSS variable: write element.style.transform on the dragged element instead.
- Sources: S-L19-005, S-L19-017, S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033, S-L19-013

### STD-performance-properties-12: Add will-change once you see the glitch
**should** · web, css, react. Add will-change: transform as the fix for an element you have seen shift 1px or jitter as its motion starts, rather than adding it by default.
- Values: fix: will-change: transform; symptom: element shifts 1px as motion starts
- Why: The cheatsheet gives will-change: transform as the fix for an element that shifts 1px as motion starts, 'only once you see it', and the practical tips give it for shaky or jittery animations. The apple-design skill instead hints it wherever motion is imminent, so this is a should.
- Sources: S-L19-013, S-L19-004

### STD-performance-properties-13: Pick the cheapest animation tool
**must** · web, css, react, react-native, ios, android. Pick the cheapest tool that fits and stop there: on the web a CSS transition, then CSS @starting-style, then a CSS animation, then WAAPI (element.animate()), then Motion; in React Native a Reanimated CSS transition, then a Reanimated CSS animation, then layout animations, then a shared value with a gesture. Never install Motion for a hover or a fade, and use Lottie only for illustration, never for UI state.
- Values: web: CSS transition (hover, press, color, state toggle) > CSS @starting-style (entry, no JS state) > CSS animation (predetermined, page busy) > WAAPI element.animate() (programmatic, no library) > Motion motion.dev (springs, layout, exit, gesture-driven values); react-native: Reanimated CSS transition (transitionProperty) > Reanimated CSS animation (animationName) > layout animations (entering / exiting / itemLayoutAnimation) > useSharedValue + Gesture + useAnimatedStyle (anything a finger touches or derived from scroll); react-native-illustration-only: lottie-react-native; react-native-huge-scene: @shopify/react-native-skia
- Why: Cheapest tool that works: don't install a motion library for a fade, and using a worklet for a two-state toggle is the mobile equivalent. Motion is for springs, layout animations, exit animations and gesture-driven values; a simple hover or fade needs only a CSS transition.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-029, S-L19-016, S-L19-015

### STD-performance-properties-14: Use IntersectionObserver instead of adding Motion
**should** · web, react. If Motion (Framer Motion) is not already in the project, detect viewport entry with the Intersection Observer API instead of adding Motion for useInView.
- Values: api: Intersection Observer API
- Why: Framer Motion is quite heavy.
- Sources: S-L19-010

### STD-performance-properties-15: CSS for predetermined motion, JS for dynamic
**should** · web, css, react. Run predetermined motion as CSS (transitions, @starting-style, keyframe animations) or WAAPI, and keep JavaScript animation (requestAnimationFrame-driven libraries or springs) for dynamic, interruptible or gesture-driven motion.
- Values: waapi-example: element.animate([{ clipPath: 'inset(0 0 100% 0)' }, { clipPath: 'inset(0 0 0 0)' }], { duration: 1000, fill: 'forwards', easing: 'cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)' })
- Why: CSS animations run off the main thread and stay smooth while the browser loads, scripts or paints, while requestAnimationFrame-based animation drops frames (a Vercel dashboard tab animation using Shared Layout Animations dropped frames during page loads until it moved to CSS). WAAPI gives JavaScript control with CSS performance: hardware-accelerated, interruptible, no library.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033, S-L19-017, S-L19-020

### STD-performance-properties-16: Treat dropped frames as a regression
**must**. Treat any animation, drag or scroll that drops frames as a failed review, measured against 60fps (120fps on displays that support it, an 8ms frame budget instead of 16ms).
- Values: baseline: 60fps; high-refresh: 120fps; frame-budget-at-120fps: 8ms
- Why: A transition that works but drops frames is a regression, not a pass; not losing frames while dragging is the starting bar, and jittery scroll reads as carelessness. 60fps is the baseline for smooth motion; newer displays run at 120fps.
- Sources: S-L19-005, S-L19-032, S-L19-027, S-L19-019, S-L19-020, S-L19-016

### STD-performance-properties-17: Virtualize long lists and large tables
**must** · web, react. Virtualize long lists and large tables so only visible rows render; never render a 1,000+ row list directly.
- Values: threshold: 1,000+ rows; library: Virtuoso (https://virtuoso.dev); if the project already uses another virtualizer such as react-window, keep it
- Why: A long list that renders everything scrolls slowly; reach for virtualization (Virtuoso) before pagination hacks.
- Sources: S-L19-013, S-L19-029

### STD-performance-properties-18: Keep React Native motion on the UI thread
**must** · react-native, ios, android. In React Native, run animation on the UI runtime with Reanimated worklets and Gesture.Pan(), never core Animated or PanResponder, and call back to the React Native runtime (scheduleOnRN) only in onEnd or a useAnimatedReaction at a threshold, never per frame.
- Values: animation: react-native-reanimated + react-native-worklets; gesture: Gesture.Pan() from react-native-gesture-handler; js-callback: scheduleOnRN in onEnd or useAnimatedReaction; wrong-thread-result: 20fps on a three-year-old Android
- Why: Animation that touches the React Native runtime stutters the moment the app does anything else and drops to 20fps on a three-year-old Android; core Animated can't follow a gesture without crossing the bridge, and scheduleOnRN in onUpdate queues a call 60 to 120 times per second.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Use Reanimated (withTiming, withSpring, useAnimatedStyle) and Gesture.Pan(); core Animated and PanResponder run on the JS thread, and scheduleOnRN belongs in onEnd or a useAnimatedReaction, not onUpdate.
- Sources: S-L19-016, S-L19-016, S-L19-016, S-L19-016, S-L19-015, S-L19-014

### STD-performance-properties-19: Crossfade static layers, not elevation or blur
**must** · react-native, ios, android. In React Native, never animate Android elevation or BlurView intensity; crossfade the opacity of a pre-shadowed layer or a static BlurView instead.
- Values: never: Android elevation, BlurView intensity; instead: opacity of a pre-shadowed layer or a static BlurView
- Why: Animating elevation re-renders the Android shadow every frame, and animating BlurView intensity re-renders the blur each frame on Android.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Crossfade the opacity of a static BlurView or a pre-shadowed layer instead of animating blur intensity or elevation.
- Sources: S-L19-016, S-L19-016

### STD-performance-properties-20: Build layout-animation builders outside render
**should** · react-native, ios, android. Define Reanimated layout-animation builders at module scope or in useMemo (a per-index delay memoized inside the row), never as an inline chain in JSX, and wrap Gesture Handler v2 gestures in useMemo the same way (v3's hook form manages its own identity).
- Values: module-scope: const ROW_CLOSE = LinearTransition.duration(200); per-index: useMemo(() => FadeInDown.duration(250).delay(index * 40), [index]); gesture-v2: useMemo(() => Gesture.Pan()..., [deps]); gesture-v3: usePanGesture({...}); onStart -> onActivate, onEnd -> onDeactivate
- Why: The Reanimated docs recommend building layout animations outside components or in useMemo: an inline chain in JSX rebuilds the builder on every render, and builders rebuilt in render cost every re-render.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Move the layout-animation builder to module scope or useMemo.
- Sources: S-L19-015, S-L19-015

### STD-performance-properties-24: Animate a child to stop hover flicker
**should** · web, css, react. When a hover effect flickers, animate a child element instead of the hovered parent.
- Why: It is the listed fix for hover-caused flicker; the source gives no further reason.
- Sources: S-L19-004

### STD-performance-properties-25: Keep per-frame movement small enough
**should**. Keep the per-frame positional change below the perception threshold to avoid strobing.
- Why: Smoothness is about what is in the frames, not just the frame rate.
- Sources: S-L19-020
